About 95bp, highest since trading began in October 2025
Source: Business Today, August 9, 2026, citing data to July 28.
That Meta's credit default swaps only began trading in October 2025 is itself a sign of the change. A company that did not borrow had no need for a market in insurance against its default.

The fourth measure is secondary prices on the riskiest paper. EnterpriseAM's October report listed the losses: the Hyperion bonds just under 92, two bonds tied to Hut 8 sites at about 94 and 92, Blackstone's QTS Project Excalibur in Georgia below 88, the Oracle Michigan campus debt at 87 and CoreWeave's unsecured bonds below 80. Ludovic Subran, chief investment officer of Allianz, told the Financial Times: "Data center bonds are having their Darwin moment, where the weakest credits struggle to survive."

Not everyone reads these signals as alarming. Iggy Ioppe, chief investment officer at Theo, told IFR: "This is a serious late-cycle signal, even if it is not yet an acute one." Ravi Shukla of Wells Fargo said: "An abrupt funding shutout looks remote." And some investors have simply stayed away. "We've generally avoided investment-grade data centre deals," said Tony Trzcinka of Impax Asset Management.

The pipeline is not shrinking. Estimates have risen all year. In January, Adweek reported that Big Tech's AI spending spree was about to get awkward, citing a Goldman Sachs estimate that Big Tech's capital spending would reach about $527 billion in 2026, up from $465 billion at the start of the third-quarter 2025 earnings season. By October, PPC Land's Decoded entry on hyperscalers put the 2026 plans of the five largest at roughly $800 billion. Moody's expects hyperscaler capital spending to reach almost $1 trillion next year, from $785 billion in 2026, and counts $2.1 trillion of contracted backlog at Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Oracle, IFR reported. Fortune noted forecasts that the five largest hyperscalers could issue $300 billion of bonds a year, against $175 billion in 2026, and JPMorgan analysts projected $375 billion of debt proceeds for SpaceX alone between 2026 and 2030. Bridgewater Associates warned in February that the AI boom had entered a "more dangerous phase."

The AI build-out is American, but its financing is increasingly global. Meta's first euro bond was cheaper than its dollar notes by about 1.55 to 1.60 percentage points at comparable maturities, which is why the company went to Frankfurt. Alphabet has borrowed in sterling, Swiss francs and, in May 2026, yen, and its century bond was denominated in sterling. Amazon set a record for the largest corporate bond ever sold in Canadian dollars in June and borrowed in Swiss francs. Each of these markets draws on a different pool of savings, and each extends the reach of AI-related credit risk into financial systems whose regulators did not choose it.

The physical build-out is spreading too. Amazon committed €33.7 billion to data centres in Spain in March 2026, PPC Land reported in August. Nscale's revenue so far comes entirely from Portugal, Norway and the United Kingdom. Japan has pledged a $33 billion gas plant for the OpenAI campus in Ohio. And the Bank of England's Financial Policy Committee named AI-related debt issuance as one of two reasons, alongside the re-escalation of conflict involving Iran, that the risk of vulnerabilities in the financial system crystallising had risen. Its Monetary Policy Committee raised Bank Rate to 4% on November 4, mainly because of energy prices, as this newsletter noted on November 7, which adds to the cost of every floating-rate loan in the chain.

Higher rates are the backdrop to everything in this edition. The Bank of England observed in September that bond yields were at their highest since 2008. Floating-rate loans, such as Nscale's GPU facilities, cost more whenever benchmark rates rise. Fixed-rate bonds issued earlier, such as Hyperion's, lose value when yields go up, which is part of the reason their prices have fallen. And every new issuer, from Meta in euros to Sopaipilla at 7.50%, has to pay the higher price of money that now prevails.

The case that AI is creating value rests on three kinds of evidence: revenue at the companies selling it, falling costs for the people using it, and early signs of higher output in the wider economy. All three exist. None of them yet matches the scale of the spending.

The revenue is real and growing fast. Anthropic, the developer of the Claude models, reported revenue of $16,956 million for the third quarter of 2026, against $1,382 million a year earlier, PPC Land reported on November 3 when it wrote that Anthropic swung to a $567m Q3 operating loss on $5bn of short-term compute, drawing on the company's amended IPO filing. Revenue for the first nine months of 2026 reached $33,242 million. More than 11,900 customers were paying at least $100,000 a year, more than 1,900 at least $1 million and about 250 at least $10 million. Models released in the previous six months produced more than 80% of the quarter's revenue. Google Cloud's revenue grew 103% in the third quarter. Microsoft said in April that its AI business had passed a $37 billion annual run rate, up 123%, PPC Land reported on September 27. Microsoft's Azure cloud grew 43% in the June quarter and passed $100 billion in annual revenue, as this newsletter noted on October 25.

In advertising, the gains are visible in pricing. Meta's average price per ad rose 14% in the third quarter, which reflects both demand and the better conversion rates its AI ranking systems produce. More than 8 million advertisers were using at least one Meta AI creative tool by the first quarter of 2026, up from 4 million at the end of 2024, PPC Land reported on May 12.

Inside the auction itself, AI's value is concrete. PPC Land's entry on inference notes that Meta's Andromeda system narrows tens of millions of candidate ads to a few thousand for each impression, and credits Meta's routing model with a 1.6% rise in conversion rates. PubMatic's Decision Fabric, launched in June 2026, returns decisions in under 10 milliseconds, and a bidder built by Bedrock has run inside Index Exchange since April 2026 within a window of under five milliseconds, in auctions that Index Exchange's chief executive has said last about 100 milliseconds. These are the uses in which the cost of a single AI decision has fallen far enough to run billions of times a day, and they are where advertising's AI returns are easiest to measure. AppLovin's growth is the clearest financial evidence that they can be large.

The cost of using AI has collapsed. The same entry cites Stanford's 2025 AI Index: the cost of querying a model at the level of GPT-3.5 fell from $20 per million tokens in November 2022 to $0.07 by October 2024. Alphabet said its Gemini serving costs fell 78% during 2025, and it was processing 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month by June 2026. The Peterson Institute for International Economics, in an analysis published on February 5, noted that the cost of solving one standard benchmark task fell from $4,500 to $11.64 over 2025. For anyone using these tools, that is an enormous gain in value. It is less obviously a gain for the companies that financed the capacity.

At the level of the economy, the clearest effect so far is the spending itself. Citi estimated that AI investment had accounted for more than half of real US GDP growth in recent quarters, Fortune reported in July. The Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, in an article published on April 14 titled Will AI investments pay off?, cited estimates that AI investment made up about 92% of GDP growth in the first half of 2025. US labour productivity rose 2.2% in 2025, and Erik Brynjolfsson of Stanford has argued that productivity growth could run at about 2.7% a year, against 1.4% over the past decade. "We're creating the potential to have massive productivity gains and a lot more wealth," he told the Richmond Fed. The Bank of England reached a similar conclusion for Britain. Its November Monetary Policy Report found that AI accounts for nearly a fifth of UK growth in 2026, mainly through firms that build, host and install AI rather than those that use it, PPC Land reported, in a finding this newsletter covered on November 7. Companies told the Bank that AI had raised their productivity by about 0.5% over three years, with almost no effect on employment. But GDP counts spending on data centres as output whether or not the data centres ever earn a return. Building a factory adds to GDP; whether the factory was worth building is a separate question.

The evidence of returns at the companies using AI is much thinner. The Richmond Fed article reported a National Bureau of Economic Research survey of about 6,000 executives in the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and Australia. Just under 70% of their firms used AI. More than 90% reported no effect on employment, and 89% reported no effect on productivity. Daron Acemoglu of MIT estimates that AI will add less than 0.55% to total factor productivity over ten years. "It is difficult to arrive at very large macroeconomic gains," he said. In a PwC survey cited by Fortune on February 2, 56% of chief executives said they had got "nothing out of" AI so far.

Marketers report the same gap. PPC Land's August 15 report on the Jane Street losses also cited a TransUnion survey, published on August 5, in which 53% of senior US marketing leaders reported meaningful returns on AI, while 89% expected to raise their AI spending, and KPMG research showing that 49% of organisations had cut back AI agent rollouts when costs outran value. A Gartner survey of 1,300 senior marketers, summarised in AdExchanger's September 8 roundup, found that roughly 60% of companies using AI would incur unexpected charges or exceed their budgets for lack of human oversight, and that 56% had deployed AI tools without clear policies. Digiday reported on July 21, under the headline "We're starting to wonder": ad industry chases AI value as usage outpaces proof, that PMG had capped token spending at $50 a day per user and that the agency Cheil had moved half its clients to pricing based on output. "Now it's moving into what actual business impact do we have," said Caroline Giegerich, vice president of AI at the IAB.

The most aggressive version of the sceptical case came from Cory Doctorow. PPC Land reported on September 27 that Cory Doctorow puts AI revenue at $50bn against $1tn of spending. His revenue estimate is not sourced, and the Anthropic and Microsoft figures above suggest it is too low for 2026. But his underlying point is about circularity: revenue of $50 billion a year is easy to generate, he argued, when a trillion dollars is being spent to produce it. "This is greater fool investment theory," he said. The same article cited Ed Zitron's estimate that OpenAI lost $20.9 billion in 2025.

Anthropic's own numbers show both sides of the argument. Revenue grew about twelvefold in a year. But compute and infrastructure costs were $9,863 million in the third quarter, 58% of revenue, and the company swung from an operating profit of $974 million in the second quarter to an operating loss of $567 million. About $5.0 billion of that compute was bought at short notice, and the filing said it "currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments." The company also gave up about $600 million of revenue in the quarter to price reductions tied to new models and contractual discounts. Adjusted operating margin fell from 19% to 15%. "At our current stage, this cycle is an inherent aspect of our business," the filing said of the need to buy compute ahead of revenue.

The developers themselves are financed mostly with equity rather than debt. IFR counted $122 billion of share sales by OpenAI and $65 billion by Anthropic in 2026 by July. Anthropic's accumulated deficit of $156.2 billion at September 30 included $135.1 billion of fair-value changes on convertible instruments, derivatives and similar securities, PPC Land noted, which means most of its reported losses reflect the rising value of its own securities rather than cash spent. The flows are circular here too. Sales through cloud marketplaces, run by the same companies that supply Anthropic's computing power, made up 44% of its revenue in the first nine months of 2026, and the top five customers accounted for about 25%. Revenue retention among existing customers was about 900%, which means the average customer spending money a year earlier was spending about nine times as much. That is extraordinary growth. It is also growth that depends on customers who are themselves spending heavily on AI.
Where the value is being destroyed

Value destruction is easier to see in some places than in others, and it is not always caused by AI alone. But several groups have lost revenue, margin or market value in ways that the companies involved attribute directly to AI.

Publishers are the most visible. PPC Land reported on November 6 that People Inc. lost 26% of core web sessions as Google AI Overviews spread. Core sessions across the 19 sites owned by the publisher of PEOPLE, Allrecipes and Investopedia fell to 1.61 billion in the third quarter of 2026 from 2.17 billion. The company's earnings presentation put AI Overviews on 82% of the searches it tracks, and its chief financial officer, Tim Quinn, said on the call that the figure was "over 90%." Digital advertising revenue fell 8% to $161.9 million. People Inc. cut 195 jobs, about 6% of its workforce, on October 29. "We've lost nearly 70% of our Google search traffic over the last few years," chief executive Neil Vogel said. "We kind of made up the term Google Zero internally." The same results showed the other side of the trade: licensing and other revenue rose 49% to $52.7 million, and non-session revenue now accounts for 43% of digital revenue. Some of the value AI takes from publishers comes back through licensing deals. For People Inc., not enough of it yet.

The damage is worse for smaller sites. Axios reported on March 17 that Chartbeat data showed small publishers lost 60% of their search traffic over two years, against 47% for medium publishers and 22% for large ones. Google Search page views fell 34% from December 2024 to December 2025. Referrals from ChatGPT rose 200%, but chatbots still accounted for less than 1% of referrals. Even when a site appears inside an AI answer, few people click through. At the end of October, Search Engine Roundtable reported on a small case study by Cyrus Shepard which found that AI Overviews and AI Mode produced an estimated click-through rate of about 0.9%, a figure Shepard himself called "not too shabby," and which this newsletter covered on October 31. Google's own network business, which pays publishers to show Google-sold ads, fell 4% to $6.97 billion in the first quarter of 2026, PPC Land reported in May, and about 90% of Google's ad revenue now comes from its own properties.

Software companies have lost market value at a speed not seen since the financial crisis. The Motley Fool reported on March 27 that software stocks had entered a bear market. The iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF fell more than 14% after Anthropic released Claude Code earlier in 2026, its worst stretch since 2008. By late March, Microsoft was down 23.3% for the year, Adobe 32.2%, Salesforce 31.3% and Shopify 26.4%. A Jefferies trader coined the term "SaaSpocalypse." "AI is not being abandoned by markets. It is being priced more carefully," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Bank. The fear behind the selloff was that AI agents would let customers build or replace the software they now rent. Private credit funds that lent more than $500 billion to software companies by the end of 2025, as Hepp noted, hold that risk too.

AI is also generating new costs for advertisers. AdExchanger reported on October 20 that AI slop sites are on the rise. A study by DecryptAds found 2,116 AI-generated recipe sites monetised with programmatic advertising. One monetisation partner, HBAgency, was listed in the ads.txt files of 1,631 of them, and Ezoic monetised 407, though Ezoic said it rejects more than 98% of the sites that apply. "Inventory that relies on deceptive authorship violates Google's guidance," said Kean Graham, chief executive of MonetizeMore. Every advertising dollar that buys a page written by a machine and read by nobody is value transferred from advertisers to site operators, with ad tech taking a cut.

Households are paying in less direct ways. The Richmond Fed noted that consumer memory prices had risen more than 170% year on year, as chipmakers diverted production to the high-bandwidth memory used in AI servers. Electricity is the larger question. Fortune reported on September 2 that a Georgia Tech study found local electricity prices rose about 5% after a data centre began operating. PPC Land's August 30 report on local opposition that blocked or delayed $156bn of data centre projects in 2025 cited an Environmental Research Letters study projecting wholesale power price increases of as much as 57% by 2030 in the worst-affected regions and 6% to 29% nationally. The same article noted counter-evidence: the consultancy E3 found no clear state-level link between load growth and rate increases, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found nominal US electricity prices rose 29% from 2019 to 2025, with the PJM grid region as the main exception.

And some investors have already lost money. Hyperion bondholders, SpaceX bondholders, CoreWeave bondholders, Jane Street and Situational Awareness are the examples above. Shareholders of Alphabet and Meta, who until recently received tens of billions a year in buybacks, are now being diluted instead: Alphabet's share count rose by 206 million in nine months.

The question of whether AI creates or destroys value is, in the end, a question about who keeps the gains. The evidence so far suggests a pattern familiar from earlier infrastructure booms: users capture much of the value, suppliers of scarce inputs capture much of the profit, and the investors who finance the capacity carry most of the risk.

The price war is the main reason. Axios reported on August 1 that DeepSeek's new bargain model accelerated AI's race to zero. DeepSeek's V4 Flash model produced output for about 28 cents that cost $25 on Anthropic's Opus 4.8, a 99% discount. OpenAI cut the price of GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% three weeks after launch. Sam Altman, OpenAI's chief executive, said: "We will have so much usage of our models that we do not need to be a gigantically high-margin business." The Peterson Institute noted that open-weight models were about 90% cheaper than closed ones but accounted for less than 30% of use, which suggests customers still pay a premium for the leading models. Anthropic's $600 million of quarterly revenue lost to price cuts shows that premium eroding.

Costs, meanwhile, are moving the other way. Alphabet's capital spending reached 40.3% of revenue in the third quarter, against 23.4% a year earlier, and every dollar of it will be depreciated through the income statement over the coming years. Anthropic's compute bill reached 58% of revenue. Nscale's cost of revenue exceeded its revenue before depreciation. CoreWeave's quarterly interest bill more than doubled. At People Inc., the digital unit's adjusted margin fell to about 23.6% in the first nine months, from 27.3% in 2025, by PPC Land's calculation. The Trade Desk guided to fourth-quarter revenue of at least $755 million and adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of at least $280 million, about 11% and 30% below the prior year's $847 million and $400 million. Teads, by contrast, found growth in connected TV, where revenue rose 37% to 12% of its total, a reminder that AI's pressure falls hardest on the businesses tied to search and web page views.

The suppliers of scarce inputs are the exception. Nvidia's chips, high-bandwidth memory, power equipment, electricians and construction workers are all in short supply, and their prices reflect it. So does the cost of capital: the banks underwriting the bonds and the private credit funds lending at 7% or more are among the clearest winners of the cycle. Outside technology, Apollo found no sign of AI lifting margins at the other 493 companies in the S&P 500, which have stayed near 10%, as this newsletter covered on October 26.

Advertisers sit in the middle. They are paying more: Meta's price per ad rose 14% in the third quarter, and a separate PPC Land analysis this week found that B2B Google click prices rose 21% with budget, position and quality held constant. Some of that buys better results, as AI ranking and creative systems raise conversion rates. Some of it, inevitably, helps pay for the platforms' capital programmes. When the companies that sell advertising spend more than their operating cash flow on AI, the advertisers who supply that cash flow are financing the build-out whether they intend to or not.

The financing chains described in this edition can be hard to hold in mind at once, so it helps to follow a single dollar. Take, as an illustration, a dollar that an advertiser spends on Meta in the autumn of 2026.

The advertiser is paying more than a year ago: Meta's average price per ad rose 14% in the third quarter. Some of that buys better results, because AI systems choose which ad to show and to whom. Meta's operating cash flow no longer covers its capital spending, so the dollar goes into the AI programme alongside borrowed money: euro bonds due in 2065, dollar notes due in 2056 and, for some campuses, bonds issued by joint ventures such as Beignet Investor, bought by funds that manage pension and insurance money.

The data centre needs chips, and much of the money flows to Nvidia, whose profits are among the clearest gains of the cycle. Nvidia, in turn, uses part of its cash to invest in, lend to and guarantee companies such as Nscale and OpenAI, which buy more Nvidia chips. The data centre needs electricity, contracted for 20 years from a power plant, and its demand on the grid can lift prices for neighbouring households. It needs construction workers and electricians, who are earning more. And it is being built partly with tax breaks granted by a state that may not disclose what they cost.

Back at the other end of the chain, the AI products that the dollar helps to fund change how people find information. Search summaries answer questions that once sent readers to publishers' sites, so People Inc. loses a quarter of its sessions and cuts jobs, and the open web's ad tech companies lose volume. Their lenders, seeing that risk, charge them more, as Yahoo found in May. Meanwhile Meta's shareholders, who once received some of the dollar back through buybacks, are instead offered non-voting shares.

At several points along that path, the dollar creates real value: better advertising, cheaper intelligence for millions of users, higher wages for skilled workers and new revenue for cloud providers. At other points, it leaves behind obligations that will last decades and are spread across pension funds, bondholders, electricity customers and taxpayers. Each of them is, in effect, betting that the chain keeps turning.

Any scorecard drawn up in the middle of an investment cycle will be wrong in places, and several of the companies below appear on both sides depending on the measure. But the evidence gathered for this edition allows a provisional ledger.
